nodes.pain_point: I don't know where to start online
inner_thoughts: I know I should be online. I've been saying that for two years. I still don't have a single listing.
A teacher I know started a Facebook page last year and now I see parents recommending her in groups. I don't know how she did it.
Every time I try to figure out where to start I get lost in too many options and give up before doing anything.
nodes.intro_body: You don't need to be on every platform. You need to be in the right two places, set up properly. Start here and you'll be further ahead than 40% of teachers in your area.

strategies.title: Start with directories — less work, more predictable
content_paragraphs: Creating a profile on Iskolaya, Panthi, Mytutor, and Advice takes 2–3 hours total. Once it's up, it stays up, works 24/7, and reaches parents who are actively searching right now.
Directories don't require ongoing posting. Set them up once, update after each result season.
Social media requires creative energy. Directories don't. Do directories first — they're the online equivalent of a sign outside your house.

visual.title: Where parents search for tuition
visual.note: 60% of teachers are already on at least one platform. Getting on 4 puts you ahead of the majority.

strategies.title: Set up a Facebook Page — not a personal profile
content_paragraphs: A Facebook Page for your tuition class is free and takes 20 minutes to set up. Name it after your subject and area: "Nugegoda O/L Mathematics — Mr. Jayawickrama."
Add your results, class times, phone number, and a real photo. Not a logo. A real photo of you teaching.
Parents search Facebook for teachers. If you're not there, they find someone else. The page doesn't need to be polished — it needs to exist.

strategies.title: Build a broadcast list from your current parents
content_paragraphs: You already have the numbers. Create a broadcast list called "Class Updates" and add every current parent.
This is your owned audience — it doesn't depend on any algorithm or platform changing its rules. Start using it immediately: class schedule for the new term, exam reminders, study tips.
One message a week is enough. That's your existing audience staying warm while you build the new one.

strategies.title: Understand which platform is for which audience
content_paragraphs: Facebook is where parents discover teachers and check credibility. WhatsApp is how they communicate day-to-day. TikTok and Instagram are where A/L students spend time — but not where they make tuition decisions.
For most teachers, Facebook + WhatsApp is the complete answer. You don't need to be everywhere.
Add other platforms only when Facebook and your directory listings are consistently generating inquiries.

cards.desc: Where parents discover and vet teachers
Where they communicate once they've decided

strategies.title: Content creation doesn't require equipment
content_paragraphs: A photo of your whiteboard with today's lesson. A result message a parent sent you (with permission, with names removed). A study tip in Sinhala typed in 2 minutes.
Good tuition content isn't cinematic — it's specific and honest. A whiteboard photo with "today we solved the hardest O/L algebra question from 2023" gets more engagement than a professional graphic.
You don't need a camera or an editor. You need a phone and something worth saying.

inner_thoughts: I posted a study tip 3 weeks ago. It got 4 likes. I don't know why I bother.
I see other teachers' posts getting shared and commented on. Mine disappear into nothing.
I've been 'building my Facebook page' for 6 months. I don't have a single inquiry from it.
nodes.intro_body: Posting without a system is how most people get stuck. A small change in what you post, when you post it, and where you post it can change everything — without posting more often.

strategies.title: The 3-post-per-week formula that actually works
content_paragraphs: Monday 7pm: a study tip or exam technique in Sinhala or Tamil. Wednesday 7pm: a student result or progress story. Friday 7pm: class schedule, upcoming exam dates, or a practical reminder.
Post when parents are scrolling — after work, after dinner. Not during school hours, not at 11am.
This isn't creative. It's consistent. And consistency at this scale beats quality when you're starting out.

strategies.title: Make content parents share, not content you want to post
content_paragraphs: Parents share two kinds of content: useful information (exam dates, study guides, preparation tips) and proof (results, student improvements, testimonials).

A post that says "Working hard builds character!" gets ignored. A post that says "3 students scored distinctions in last week's O/L practice paper — proud of this batch" gets shared by parents to other parents.
Every post should answer one question: would a parent share this with another parent? If not, rewrite it.

strategies.title: Community groups are where discovery actually happens
content_paragraphs: Every area has WhatsApp groups and Facebook groups for parents: "Rajagiriya Parents", school community groups, "Anuradhapura Mothers Network." Join them. Answer questions about exams, study strategies, school calendars.
Don't advertise. Help. When someone eventually asks "does anyone know a good chemistry teacher near Nugegoda?" — your name will already be familiar from weeks of helpful answers.
Familiarity built over time converts when the moment arrives.

strategies.title: Run one small Facebook ad during enrollment season
content_paragraphs: LKR 2,000–5,000 for a 7-day boosted post is enough to reach 3,000–5,000 parents in your area. Choose January (peak enrollment) or August (crash course season).
Boost a post with your best recent results — pass rates, grade counts, a student quote. Not a class schedule. Results.
This is not a big investment. It's enough to test whether paid reach works for you before committing more.

strategies.title: Measure inquiries, not likes
content_paragraphs: Likes don't pay fees. Track how many new parent inquiries you get each month — and note which posts they mentioned seeing.
After 3 months of consistent posting, you'll know exactly which type of content brings inquiries. Double down on that. Stop making the rest.
A results post that gets 8 likes and 3 inquiries beats an inspirational post that gets 40 likes and zero inquiries every time.

nodes.pain_point: I want to teach online but don't know how
inner_thoughts: I have students outside my area who want to join my class. But I don't know how to do it properly.
I spent an hour trying to get Zoom working before my first online session. Three students couldn't connect and I gave up.
I don't know what to charge for online classes. The same as physical? Less? I have no idea.
nodes.intro_body: Online teaching is simpler than the setup anxiety makes it seem. Once the first session runs without problems, it becomes routine quickly. Here's the setup that works first time.

strategies.title: Zoom is the tool — here's the setup that works first time
content_paragraphs: Free Zoom allows 40-minute sessions (enough for practice, not full classes). Zoom Pro at LKR 1,500–2,000/month removes the time limit. Install on your tablet or laptop — not just your phone.

Do a test session with one trusted parent before your first real online class. 15 minutes. Check audio, screen sharing, and reconnection after a drop. This prevents the 3-student-connectivity disaster on launch day.
Settings to configure once: set a meeting password, enable waiting room, turn off participant screen sharing, mute participants on entry.

strategies.title: Price online classes at 60–70% of your physical rate
content_paragraphs: Online students don't get the in-person attention, the physical classroom energy, or the ability to walk up to you after class with their book. The price should reflect that.
At 60–70% of your physical rate, the difference is fair and transparent. A physical class at LKR 3,000/month becomes LKR 2,000–2,100 online.
That's still meaningful revenue for zero hall costs and zero travel time. And it lets you reach students outside your area who couldn't attend physically.

cards.desc: Of physical rate for online classes

strategies.title: Record sessions as catch-up content
content_paragraphs: With student and parent consent, record your Zoom sessions. Students who miss a class can watch it back — they don't fall behind, they don't drop.

Recording solves the single biggest disadvantage of online tuition compared to physical. A student who misses a physical class is behind. A student who misses a recorded online class watches it back over the weekend.
This isn't free labor. It's a retention tool that costs zero extra time.

strategies.title: Start a YouTube channel for long-term lead generation
content_paragraphs: 10-minute subject explainers in Sinhala or Tamil — one per week. Build a searchable library of your best teaching.
A parent Googling "A/L physics wave motion Sri Lanka Sinhala" and finding your video is a warm lead who's already seen how you teach before they contact you.
This is a 12-month game: month 1 you have 4 videos, month 12 you have 52 — and new students find you while you sleep.

strategies.title: Understand the digital divide — online supplements, it doesn't replace
content_paragraphs: About 30% of Sri Lankan students still have no reliable internet access, particularly in rural areas. For these students, online-only isn't an option.

The hybrid model — physical class with an online version running in parallel — gives you the broadest reach. Rural students attend physically; Colombo students join online. Same session, different channels.
Online is your scaling lever, not your replacement strategy.

cards.desc: Of students still lack reliable internet access
Physical + online is the broadest-reach model

strategies.title: Use existing platforms to reach beyond your geography
content_paragraphs: Online listing platforms like OnlineTuition.lk, Siplo.lk (1,220+ qualified teachers), and TeacherOn.com (6,000+ SL tutors listed) have existing parent traffic. Listing on them doesn't replace your own channels — it adds to them.
These platforms are useful for reaching parents in districts where you have zero word-of-mouth presence yet.
Set up a profile once, keep it updated with current results, and let it work in the background.
